narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Yapong dance was first performed to prepare for the 450th anniversary of the city of Jakarta in 1977.
Artist Bagong Kussudiarjo organized the event after conducting months of research into Betawi life via libraries, films, and direct observation.
The premiere took place at the Senayan Convention Center with 300 performers.
on_screen: Map: Indonesia · Southeast Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally part of a ballet about Prince Jayakarta, it now depicts the association of young people.
It is performed to enliven anniversaries and festive events, symbolizing joy and the welcoming of significant figures.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features dynamic and exotic movements intended to show a happy atmosphere.
It is a blend of Betawi folk dance, pop dance elements, and Sumatran dance influences.
The movements were originally designed to depict the welcoming of Prince Jayakarta.
Watch for Yapong Step.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is a mixture of Betawi, Javanese, and Sundanese elements.
Specific instruments used include the Rebana Biang, Rebana Hadroh, and Rebana Ketimpring.
Listen for the Rebana Biang, Rebana Hadroh, Rebana Ketimpring, Javanese instruments.
A rhythmic blend of traditional Betawi frame drums (rebana) with Javanese and Sundanese melodic influences, characterized by a call-and-response feel between singers and percussion.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes are based on Betawi mask dancer attire, including a headgear and a chest sash called toka-toka.
The fabric often features bright red colors and dragon motifs, reflecting Chinese cultural influence in Jakarta.
on_screen: Image gallery: 8 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Bagong Kussudiardja is the central figure, having created the dance and conducted the foundational research for its choreography and staging in 1977.
While primarily a Betawi dance from Jakarta, it incorporates elements from Sumatran, Javanese, and Sundanese traditions.
The dance is a 'new creation' that departs from traditional Betawi movements but is heavily influenced by Betawi mask dance (Tari Topeng Betawi) and Chinese-Indonesian aesthetics.
